topics: Root cause: autoscaler race condition & KV cache retention
Mitigations applied: emergency rollback, rate-limiting, temp smaller model routing
Planned fixes: autoscaler hotfix, KV compaction, improved alerts
Reliability roadmap: canaries, runbooks, SLOs, Dedicated capacity discussion
Security/compliance questions: logs retention, audit trail
transcript:
Header: 2027-01-08 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~42m | Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Liam (CSM), Carlos (Sable VP Eng), Asha (SRE), Nina (PM)

Summary: quick reconfirmation then dive into details. Transcript quality medium, some auto-captions off.

00:00 Speaker 1 (Jordan): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you making time this afternoon. We're here to walk through the postmortem follow up from the Dec twenty-eighth incident. Maya has the timeline and the proposed fixes.
00:18 Speaker 2 (Maya): yeah hi all, um so quick recap: roughly 14:02 UTC we started seeing request latency climb on the gen endpoints, by 14:06 error rates increased. Our initial mitigation was to route traffic to the smaller model variant and apply a global rate limit while we investigated. That bought us stability but not full mitigation.
00:36 Speaker 3 (Carlos): can you rewind a little — why did the autoscaler not spin up capacity? we had multiple pods at 100 percent, we saw queuing, why weren't new instances created?
00:50 Speaker 2 (Maya): so, what we found in the logs — and okay this is slightly messy — is there was a race in the autoscaler module when high-churn short lived pods were created. the scaler evaluated pod templates and hit a fast-path that skipped the scale up because it thought the pool had warm capacity, but the KV cache priming was still ongoing and memory climbed. in short: scale decision was based on stale metrics.
01:12 Speaker 1 (Jordan): to add, the memory growth in the K V cache caused OOM pressure so some of the long-lived workers restarted, which further confused the scaler. it was a feedback loop.
01:24 Speaker 4 (Asha): we saw the policy that keeps prefix cache for 30 minutes; with this workload the prefix cardinality exploded. is there a mitigation for the cache retention?
01:40 Speaker 2 (Maya): yes, we pushed a short term config change during the incident to reduce retention to 2 minutes for the worst-affected routes, which lowered memory growth. longer term we plan an eviction/compaction algorithm and per-route cache caps.
01:54 Speaker 3 (Carlos): you mentioned smaller model routing — did that change quality for end-users? we have clinical notes ingestion and accuracy matters.
02:07 Speaker 2 (Maya): some drop in token-level quality for the heavy prompt set, but we had a fallback policy to only route non-critical routes to the smaller variant and keep critical routes on the original model where possible. we also logged outputs to evaluate for regression; initial checks show negligible clinical-impact but we want to be thorough.
02:25 Speaker 5 (Nina): and about Dedicated — we asked earlier about reserving capacity to avoid noisy neighbor effects, is that still recommended?
02:36 Speaker 1 (Jordan): Dedicated helps if you want isolation and predictable throughput; however Dedicated won't solve the autoscaler race fundamentally in the serving runtime — it reduces interference from other customers though. For immediate reliability we recommended a combination: short-term hotfixes + consider Dedicated for production-critical pipelines.
02:58 Speaker 4 (Asha): ok what about Private / on-prem? we have strict data residency. you said there were some platform telemetry pieces that would need handshake for Private?
03:12 Speaker 2 (Maya): correct — Private has the option to opt out of certain control-plane telemetry; we can supply audit logs and local KMS integration. during the incident we used tracing that lives in the control plane which in Private you'd host locally. we'll send the outline of what traces we need to retain vs optional.
03:30 Speaker 3 (Carlos): quick question on alerting — our oncall didn't get the right pager; it fired but threshold was too high — can you propose alerting thresholds that would have caught the gradual memory growth earlier?
03:43 Speaker 2 (Maya): yes, part of our remediation is to add an early-warning metric: "kv_cache_unique_prefixes" and a rolling 5m growth rate alert. also a derived signal combining queue depth and pod restart count. We'll share suggested thresholds tuned to your baseline.
04:02 Speaker 1 (Jordan): okay let's go through the timeline again quick and the actions taken. Maya, can you speak to the hotfix and the plan for deployment and verification?
04:12 Speaker 2 (Maya): hotfix is a guard in the autoscaler to avoid decisions based on metrics older than 60s and a small change to the evaluation window to account for transient restarts. we've validated in staging with synthetic churn and mem growth and it prevents the skip. next steps: deploy to canary pool, run the 10k rps workload for 30m, check memory and restart metrics.
04:38 Speaker 4 (Asha): what's the rollback plan if the hotfix causes unexpected behavior?
04:44 Speaker 2 (Maya): the change toggles via a feature flag and we can immediately flip back; canary is isolated to a small set of machines and we have circuit-breakers on the scaler decisions.
04:56 Speaker 1 (Jordan): Customer asked also for improved runbooks. Liam?
05:02 Speaker 6 (Liam): yeah we will produce a runbook that includes steps to mitigate: reduce cache retention, apply rate-limits, route to smaller variants, and how to trigger emergency fallback. we'll include playbook commands for SRE teams and examples for PagerDuty routing.
05:18 Speaker 3 (Carlos): thanks. in terms of timeline — when can we expect the patch in production?
05:24 Speaker 2 (Maya): we're aiming to push to staging by 2027-01-12, canary on 2027-01-13, and prod rollout 2027-01-14 if canary is clean. we'll drop the links in the follow-up mail.
05:38 Speaker 4 (Asha): and the KV compaction — is that a bigger change? when would that land?
05:45 Speaker 2 (Maya): compaction is medium effort — target Q1 deliverable; we'll have an interim mitigation (per-route caps and TTL adjustments) in two weeks.
05:56 Speaker 5 (Nina): for auditing and compliance, do you have an export of the incident timeline and who accessed what logs? we need it for our internal review.
06:07 Speaker 1 (Jordan): yes, we'll include a redacted access log extract and the timeline slides; also attach SOC2 control mappings relevant to the incident response.
06:18 Speaker 3 (Carlos): any blockers on your side to deliver these items?
06:23 Speaker 2 (Maya): no blockers; engineering prioritization is underway and we have a small team assigned. we'll need the synthetic workload profile from Sable to tune thresholds.
06:34 Speaker 4 (Asha): I'll share that today.
06:36 Speaker 1 (Jordan): great. recap of next steps — we'll send the postmortem doc, the runbook draft, the autoscaler patch schedule, and the canary test plan. follow-up checkin 2027-01-18. thanks all.
06:58 Speaker 3 (Carlos): thanks, appreciate the quick follow through.
07:04 Speaker 6 (Liam): thanks everyone, we'll get the notes out within 24 hours.
07:10 End of recording.
